This tutorial explores the use of NEON breeding landbird data for occupancy modeling. The focus is on preparing observational bird data, constructing detection histories, and fitting single- and multi-season occupancy models. Although birds are used here as the example, the same workflow can be applied to other organismal <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/data-collection/observational-sampling" target="_blank">NEON observational sampling datasets</a> that provide species-level detections. If you are interested in linking occupancy results with environmental predictors, the methods demonstrated here can also be extended to incorporate covariates from NEON data products that describe habitat structure or climate, such as those derived from <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/data-collection/automated-instruments" target="_blank">NEON's Automated Instrument Systems</a>.

<div id="ds-objectives" markdown="1">

## Learning Objectives 
After completing this tutorial you will be able to: 

* Understand the basics of occupancy modeling.
* Prepare NEON breeding landbird data for occupancy analysis and build detection histories.
* Fit occupancy models in R and interpret occupancy and detection estimates.
* Incorporate site-level and survey-level covariates to evaluate factors influencing detection and occupancy.

## Things You’ll Need To Complete This Tutorial

### R Programming Language
You will need a current version of R to complete this tutorial. We also recommend 
the RStudio IDE to work with R. 

</div>

## Introduction to NEON Bird Observations
NEON’s breeding landbird point count dataset provides taxonomic identifications, distances, and detection information for all birds observed during standardized six-minute surveys. The protocol focuses on diurnal, terrestrial breeding landbirds, a group chosen because they respond strongly to changes in climate, habitat, and land use, and because they interact with other NEON-monitored organisms.

Field crews survey spatially distributed locations during the breeding season, recording every bird seen or heard. These repeated surveys across years and sites produce rich detection–nondetection data suited for occupancy modeling and for exploring how bird communities vary across environmental gradients.

NEON’s terrestrial field **sites** are designated as *large* or *small*, which determines the sampling design. Large sites are surveyed once per year and contain 5–10 **plots** containing Bird Grids, each made up of a 3×3 array of nine **points** spaced 250 m apart (see Figure). Field crews visit every point in a grid and conduct a 6-minute **point-count survey**. Smaller sites, which cannot accommodate full grids, are surveyed twice per year and contain 2–25 point-count locations that are randomly distributed across the site and spaced at least 250 m apart.

<div id="ds-dataTip" markdown="1">
<i class="fa fa-star"></i> **Data Tip:** NEON’s bird data follow a hierarchical structure: DomainID → SiteID → PlotID → PointID. Large sites use points labeled 1–9, while small sites use point label 21 for all locations.
For example: (Large Site) D07 → GRSM → GRSM_002 → 5 | (Small Site) D20 → PUUM → PUUM_001 → 21.
</div> 

<figure>
	<a href="https://github.com/anushkakg/Bird-Occupancy-Modeling/tree/main/images/birdGrid.jpg">
	<img src="https://github.com/anushkakg/Bird-Occupancy-Modeling/tree/main/images/birdGrid.jpg" alt="Design of the bird point count grid, consisting of 9 points separated by a minimum of 250 m."></a>

	</figcaption>
</figure>

More details on NEON’s bird monitoring program are available on the <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/data-collection/birds" target="_blank">NEON bird resource page</a>. Protocols referenced in the data can be found in the <a href="https://data.neonscience.org/documents" target="_blank">Document Library</a>.

## Introduction to Occupancy Modeling
When searching for a species, there are technically three possible outcomes:

1. The species is present and you detect it,
2. the species is present and you do not detect it, or
3. the species is absent and therefore not detected.

Traditional presence–absence data cannot distinguish missed detections from true absences, which introduces uncertainty. Occupancy modeling addresses this challenge by explicitly modeling two linked processes: the true **occupancy** of the species and the **probability** of detecting the species given that it is present.

This framework estimates two key parameters:

* the probability that a site is occupied by a species (ψ)
* the probability of detecting the species during a survey, given that it is present (p). 

To tease apart ψ and p, the model requires repeated surveys of the same site within a period when occupancy of a species is assumed not to change. NEON’s observational sampling design is ideal for this approach, because surveys include repeated, standardized visits to locations across years.

## Importing NEON Data

First, we’ll download the breeding landbird data product (<a href="https://data.neonscience.org/data-products/DP1.10003.001" target="_blank">DP1.10003.001</a>) for all NEON terrestrial field sites included in <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/data-samples/data-management/data-revisions-releases/release-2025" target="_blank">RELEASE-2025</a>. 

* NEON (National Ecological Observatory Network). Breeding landbird point counts (DP1.10003.001), RELEASE-2025. <a href="https://doi.org/10.48443/3nka-yg96" target="_blank">https://doi.org/10.48443/3nka-yg96</a>. Dataset accessed in R via neonUtilities on <span id="access-date"></span>.

<script>
  const options = { year: 'numeric', month: 'long', day: 'numeric' };
  document.getElementById("access-date").textContent =
    new Date().toLocaleDateString(undefined, options);
</script>

On the first run, this code block will download the full dataset for all sites. Because the data product is large and spans multiple years-including years before some sites became operational-the initial download may take some time. A cached version of the dataset is saved locally, so on re-run, the code simply loads the local file instead of downloading the data again.

A NEON token is used to download the original data for this workflow. Tokens are optional but recommended, as they allow authenticated access and help avoid API rate limits when downloading large datasets. For more information, see the <a href="https://www.neonscience.org/resources/learning-hub/tutorials/neon-api-tokens-tutorial" target="_blank">Using an API Token when Accessing NEON Data with neonUtilities tutorial</a> and the <a href="https://data.neonscience.org/data-api/rate-limiting/#api-tokens" target="_blank">NEON API token documentation</a>.

```{r import}
# Define NEON sites
large_sites <- c(
  "BARR", "BART", "BONA", "CLBJ", "CPER", "DEJU", "DSNY", "GRSM",
  "GUAN", "HARV", "HEAL", "JERC", "JORN", "KONZ", "MLBS", "MOAB",
  "NIWO", "OAES", "ONAQ", "ORNL", "OSBS", "RMNP", "SJER", "SRER",
  "STEI", "TALL", "TEAK", "UKFS", "UNDE", "WOOD", "WREF", "YELL"
)
small_sites <- c(
  "DELA", "LENO", "TOOL", "SOAP", "STER", "PUUM", "KONA",
  "SERC", "DCFS", "NOGP", "LAJA", "BLAN", "SCBI", "ABBY", "TREE"
)
sites <- c(large_sites, small_sites)

# Set up directories
if (!dir.exists("data")) {
  dir.create("data")
}
if (!dir.exists("outputs")) {
  dir.create("outputs")
}

# Path to cached dataset
bird_counts_path <- file.path("data", "bird_counts.RData")

# Load cached data if available; otherwise download and save
if (file.exists(bird_counts_path)) {
  load(bird_counts_path)
} else {
  bird.counts <- loadByProduct(
    dpID    = "DP1.10003.001",
    package = "basic",
    release = "RELEASE-2025",
    token   = Sys.getenv("NEON_TOKEN"),
    site    = sites,
    check.size = FALSE
  )
  
  save(bird.counts, file = bird_counts_path)
}
```

## Preparing the Data

NEON provides separate tables for point-count survey metadata (`brd_perpoint`) and the bird counts themselves (`brd_countdata`).

Take a look at their structure (that is, what fields are included) and the data in them. We can see that `brd_perpoint` contains metadata fields describing the location, elevation, date and field-crew recorded weather conditions for each point-count survey. 

```{r brd_perpoint}
str(bird.counts$brd_perpoint)

head(bird.counts$brd_perpoint, n=10)
```

`brd_countdata` contains data for the birds observed during each point-count survey, including identification, observation method, distance, and minutes where no birds were observed.

```{r brd_countdata}
str(bird.counts$brd_countdata)

head(bird.counts$brd_countdata, n=10)
```

Before we can fit occupancy models, we need to clean the data a bit. This includes:

* Creating a unique identifier for each point-count survey.
* Filtering out incomplete point-count surveys.
* Keeping only detections identified to the species level.
* Removing duplicate point-count surveys.
* Joining the two tables into a single dataset.

### Create a unique point-count survey ID

Each point-count survey needs a unique identifier so that we can match the detection data (brd_countdata) with the corresponding per-point metadata (brd_perpoint). We extract the survey year from eventID and then combine the plot, point, year, and bout into a single key called pointSurveyID for each of the tables. Note, because the siteID is already included in the plotID (e.g., BART_012), siteID is not included in the construction of `pointSurveyID`.

```{r uniqueIdentifier}
brd_perpoint_clean <- bird.counts$brd_perpoint %>%
  mutate(year = str_extract(eventID, "\\d{4}"))%>%
  mutate(pointSurveyID = paste(plotID, "point", pointID, year, "bout", boutNumber, sep = "_"))

brd_countdata_clean <- bird.counts$brd_countdata %>%
  mutate(year = str_extract(eventID, "\\d{4}"))%>%
  mutate(pointSurveyID = paste(plotID, "point", pointID, year, "bout", boutNumber, sep = "_"))
```

### Remove incomplete surveys

The `samplingImpractical` field flags point-count surveys that could not be completed (e.g., weather, access issues). For our purposes, we keep only surveys marked as "OK".

```{r}
brd_perpoint_clean <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(samplingImpractical == "OK")
```

### Keep only species-level records

For this workflow, we only focus on detections identified to the species level. Records that are not identified to species (or have `NA` in `taxonRank`) are dropped.

```{r}
brd_countdata_clean <- brd_countdata_clean %>%
  filter(taxonRank == "species")
```

### Remove duplicate surveys

Each `pointSurveyID` should correspond to a single point-count survey. Occasionally, duplicate IDs appear, likely due to data entry or processing issues. We identify any duplicated `pointSurveyID` values and remove those surveys from both tables.

```{r}
duplicate_pointSurveyID <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  count(pointSurveyID) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  pull(pointSurveyID)

brd_perpoint_clean <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(!pointSurveyID %in% duplicate_pointSurveyID)

brd_countdata_clean <- brd_countdata_clean %>%
  filter(!pointSurveyID %in% duplicate_pointSurveyID)
```

### Join per-point and count tables

Finally, we join the cleaned detection data (`brd_countdata_clean`) with the cleaned per-point metadata (`brd_perpoint_clean`) using `pointSurveyID` as the primary key. After the join, we drop duplicate columns and keep a single, combined dataset.

```{r}
brd_joineddata_clean <- inner_join(
  brd_countdata_clean,
  brd_perpoint_clean,
  by = "pointSurveyID",
  suffix = c(".count", ".perpoint")
)

#Remove duplicate columns between tables
brd_joineddata_clean <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  select(-matches("\\.perpoint$"))
names(brd_joineddata_clean) <- gsub("\\.count$", "", names(brd_joineddata_clean))
```


## Descriptive Analyses

Great, now that our data are cleaned and standardized, we can start doing some basic analyses. First, lets take a look at a single species within a site in terms of its detection and occupancy. 

### Single-season Occupancy Model

#### Single Species

We have chosen to look at Melanerpes carolinus (Red-bellied Woodpecker) across all sites

##### Data Munging

##### Occupancy Table

```{r}
# Filter table by species
bird_species <- "Melanerpes carolinus"
brd_joineddata_model1 <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% sites) %>%
  filter(scientificName == bird_species)

# Get all valid surveys years across sites (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  distinct(siteID, year)

# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a site* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model1 %>%
  group_by(siteID, year) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")

# Join and fill
site_by_year <- valid_site_years %>%
  left_join(detections, by = c("siteID", "year")) %>%
  mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = present
  )

head(site_by_year, n=10)
```

#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
```{r}
birds_pao_model1 <- createPao(
  data = site_by_year[, c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")],
  unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
  title = "Red-bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
```{r}
birds_occupancy_model1 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model1,           
  model = list(
    psi ~ 1,  
    p ~ 1),
  type = 'so'
  )

summary(birds_occupancy_model1)
```

#### Model Results

This shows that Melanerpes carolinus has an occupancy probability (psi) of 45% (i.e., if you go to any of these sites, there is a 45% chance of this bird occupying the site) and a detection probability (p) of 91% (i.e., if you visit a site and the bird occupies it, there is a 91% chance you will detect it)

```{r}
#print_one_site_estimates(mod = birds_occupancy_model1, site = 1)

#fitted(object = birds_occupancy_model1, param = 'psi', prob = 0.95)
#fitted(object = birds_occupancy_model1, param = 'p', prob = 0.95)

ests <- as.data.frame(print_one_site_estimates(mod = birds_occupancy_model1))

ests <- ests[1:2,] %>% 
  mutate(parm = c("psi", "p")) %>% 
  select(parm, est, se, lower, upper) %>% 
  rename(., 
    c(
      Parameter = parm,
      Estimate = est,
      SE = se,
      L95 = lower,
      U95 = upper
    )
  ) %>% 
  `rownames<-`(seq_len(nrow(ests[1:2,])))

ests
```


```{r}
ggplot(ests, aes(x = Parameter, y = Estimate)) +
  labs(x = "Parameter", y = "Estimate") +
  geom_bar(stat = 'identity') +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = L95, ymax = U95), width = 0.2) +
  theme_bw()
```

### Across all Species

#### Create a function
todo: change the vars to be just in scope for the function
```{r, message=FALSE}
run_occ_for_species_list <- function(species_df, brd_joineddata_clean, brd_perpoint_clean, sites, years = c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")) {
  
  results <- list()
  detection_histories <- list()
  
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(species_df))) {
    
    sci_name <- species_df$scientificName[i]
    common_name <- species_df$vernacularName[i]
    
    # Filter detection data to this species and the sites
    brd_species <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
      filter(siteID %in% sites, scientificName == sci_name)
    
    # Get valid surveys (site-year combos with effort)
    valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
      filter(siteID %in% sites) %>%
      distinct(siteID, year)
    
    # Get detections for this species
    detections <- brd_species %>%
      group_by(siteID, year) %>%
      summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")
    
    # Build site-year detection matrix
    site_by_year <- valid_site_years %>%
      left_join(detections, by = c("siteID", "year")) %>%
      mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
      pivot_wider(
        names_from = year,
        values_from = present
      )
    
    # Create Pao object
    birds_pao <- createPao(
      data = site_by_year[, years],
      unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
      title = common_name
    )
    
    # Run occupancy model
    model <- occMod(
      data = birds_pao,
      model = list(psi ~ 1, p ~ 1),
      type = "so"
    )
    
    # Extract estimates
    ests <- print_one_site_estimates(mod = model) %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      slice(1:2)
    
    rownames(ests) <- NULL
    
    named_est <- list(
      vernacularName = common_name,
      psi_Estimate = ests$est[1],
      psi_SE       = ests$se[1],
      psi_L95      = ests$lower[1],
      psi_U95      = ests$upper[1],
      p_Estimate   = ests$est[2],
      p_SE         = ests$se[2],
      p_L95        = ests$lower[2],
      p_U95        = ests$upper[2]
    )

    detection_histories[[sci_name]] <- site_by_year
    results[[sci_name]] <- named_est
  }
  
  return(list(
    estimates = results,
    detection_histories = detection_histories
  ))
  
}
```

Run the function across all species

```{r warning=FALSE}
species_input <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  distinct(scientificName, vernacularName) %>%
  arrange(scientificName)

results_df <- run_occ_for_species_list(
  species_df = species_input,
  brd_joineddata_clean = brd_joineddata_clean,
  brd_perpoint_clean = brd_perpoint_clean,
  sites = sites
)
```

### Adding Covariates
Detectability and occupancy of a species can be influenced by many different random effects, such as:

Survey characteristics:

* The observer: some observers may be better at spotting individuals of a species that are particularly camouflaged to their environments

* The weather: adverse weather conditions such as rain or snow can impact visibility during a study, and therefore impact detection probability

Site characteristics: sites with heavy cover or dense forests may decrease detection probability and make it harder for observers to identify the species

* Example: Sitka black-tailed deer that live in the boreal forests in southeast Alaska may be harder to spot than mule deer living in more open ecosystems in Nevada

We can include data about these characteristics in our model to either a) describe previously known variation and thereby improve the model fit or b) test to see whether occupancy/detection of a site is a function of a covariate.

#### Occupancy Covariates
These are covariates that influence occupancy of a species. Occupancy probability can only be influenced by site characteristics.

For example, shorebird occupancy would benefit from data on the extent of tidal flats, seabirds distributions are often influenced by ocean depth, and in many regions elevation plays a critical role in determining site occupancy.

Melanerpes carolinus (Red-bellied Woodpecker) across all sites

##### Covariants
We use the same occupancy table as above, but we need to create a table with the site covariates (aka nlcdClass).

```{r}
#categorical
#site_cov <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
#  select(siteID, nlcdClass) %>%
#  distinct(siteID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
#  mutate(nlcdClass = as.factor(nlcdClass)) %>%
#  tibble::column_to_rownames("siteID")

#non-categorical
site_cov <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  select(siteID, elevation) %>%
  distinct(siteID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("siteID")
```

#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
```{r}
birds_pao_model2 <- createPao(
  data = site_by_year[, c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")],
  unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
  unitcov = site_cov,
  title = "Red-bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
```{r}
birds_occupancy_model2 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model2,           
  model = list(psi ~ elevation,  p ~ 1),
  type = 'so'
  )
```

#### Model Results

```{r}
mod.list <-  list(
    birds_occupancy_model1, 
    birds_occupancy_model2
)
aictable <- createAicTable(mod.list = mod.list)
aictable$table
```
Looking at the two models, we can briefly look at the AIC values. The AIC for the model with elevation is lower (better), so the principle of parsimony suggests this is the better model: it is the more parsimonous model when considering both fit and number of parameters.

We see that compared to the original model that did not account for elevation there are 3 parameters vs 2. We can calculate a p value to quantify how much better of a fit this model is.

```{r}
#get the difference in the neg2loglike between the two models
diff <- abs(birds_occupancy_model1$neg2loglike - birds_occupancy_model2$neg2loglike)

#look up our observed difference on a chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom to get p value
pchisq(diff, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

```
A p value of 2.356024e-05 is low so we can confidently reject the null hypothesis.

```{r}
coef(birds_occupancy_model2, param = 'psi')

data <- cbind(site_cov, birds_occupancy_model2$real$psi) %>% 
  distinct(.keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  arrange(elevation)

ggplot(data, aes(x = elevation, y = est)) +
  geom_point() + 
  labs(x = "Elevation",
       y = "Predicted Occupancy") +
  lims(y = c(0, 1))
```

#### Detection Covariates
Covariates can also be unique for each site as well as each survey.

It is important to recognize that detection probability can be influenced by either survey characteristics or site characteristics.

We are going to see whether temperature of the survey affects the detection of calling Red-bellied Woodpeckers.

#### Data Munging

##### Occupancy Table
By plot this time, not site since an entire site is not surveyed in a single survey, only a plot is

```{r}
# Filter table by species
bird_species <- "Setophaga virens"

#unique(brd_joineddata_clean$detectionMethod)

brd_joineddata_model3 <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  filter(scientificName == bird_species) %>%
  filter(detectionMethod %in% c("singing", "calling", "other aural (e.g. wing beats)", "drumming", "calling and singing", "other aural and singing"))

# Get all valid surveys years across sites (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_plot_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  distinct(plotID, year)
  
# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a site* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model3 %>%
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")
  
# Join and fill
plot_by_year <- valid_plot_years %>%
  left_join(detections, by = c("plotID","year")) %>%
  mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = present
  ) %>%
  select(1, sort(names(.)[-1])) %>%
  arrange(plotID)

head(plot_by_year, n=10)

```

##### Covariants

observedAirTemp
```{r}
observedAirTemp_surveys <- brd_joineddata_clean %>% #this needs to be from the whole dataset, since environmental variables are not dependent on bird detection
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(
    observedAirTemp = na_if(mean(observedAirTemp, na.rm = TRUE), NaN),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = observedAirTemp
  ) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames('plotID') %>%
  select(sort(names(.)))

```

kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed

```{r}
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
  group_by(plotID, year) %>%
  summarize(
    kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed = na_if(mean(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, na.rm = TRUE), NaN),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed
  ) %>%

```

cloudCover

```{r}
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%

  summarize(
    cloudCover = na_if(mean((startCloudCoverPercentage + endCloudCoverPercentage) / 2, na.rm = TRUE), NaN),
```

```{r}
  filter(siteID %in% large_sites) %>%
```

Create survey Cov

Note: this has all 4 in it but we do not have to use all 4 in the model or final tutorial
```{r}
# create the surveycov dataframe
surveycov <-  data.frame(
  observedAirTemp = unlist(observedAirTemp_surveys),
  kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed = unlist(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed_surveys),
  cloudCover = unlist(cloudCover_surveys),
  relativeHumidity = unlist(relativeHumidity_surveys)
  )

# remove the rownames
row.names(surveycov) <- NULL

head(surveycov)

```


#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
```{r}
birds_pao_model3 <- createPao(
  data = plot_by_year[, c("2018", "2019", "2020", "2021", "2022", "2023")],
  unitnames = plot_by_year$plotID,
  survcov = surveycov,
  title = "Red-Bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
There will be a warning since we are missing some env variable values where we have detection data (i guess for some reason they didn't record it sometimes)
```{r}
birds_occupancy_model3 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model3,           
  model = list(psi ~ 1,  p ~ kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed),
  type = 'so'
  )

summary(birds_occupancy_model3)
```

#### Model Results

```{r}
coef(birds_occupancy_model3, 'p')

```
Here, we can see that the beta estimate for kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed is slightly negative (i.e., as windspeed increases, detection for calling birds decreases) and 0 is not included in the confidence interval, so there is a statistically significant effect that windspeed affects detection

Remember, these coefficients are on the (unbounded) logit scale. The standard error is provided for each estimate, as are the 95% confidence intervals. The confidence intervals can be computed by hand as the estimate +/- 1.96 times the standard error. If the confidence interval encompasses 0, traditionally we say the estimate is “not statistically significant”. If the beta could reasonably be 0, it means the variable has no effect (or at least we don’t have evidence of its effect in the dataset).

Lets plot something
```{r}
newdata <- data.frame(
  kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed = seq(from = min(unlist(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed_surveys), na.rm = TRUE),
             to = max(unlist(kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed_surveys), na.rm = TRUE),
             by = 1)
  )
predictions <- predict(birds_occupancy_model3, newdata, 'p')
predictions$kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed <- newdata$kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed
  
# plot the predictions with ggplot2
ggplot(data = predictions, aes(x = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, y = est)) +
 geom_line() +
 geom_line(aes(x = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, y = lower_0.95), linetype = "dashed") +
 geom_line(aes(x = kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed, y = upper_0.95), linetype = "dashed") +
 labs(x = "kmPerHourObservedWindSpeed", 
      y = "Predicted detection") +
 lims(y = c(0, 1))
```

###  Multi-season Occupancy Model

While the single-season occupancy model assumes that the sites are closed to 
changes in occupancy state over the study, we may want to know how occupancy rates are changing over time. For this we use the multi-season occupancy model.

#### Single Species

Melanerpes carolinus (Red-bellied Woodpecker) across all sites

#### Data Munging

##### Occupancy Table

```{r}
# Filter table by species
bird_species <- "Melanerpes carolinus"
brd_joineddata_model4 <- brd_joineddata_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% small_sites) %>%
  filter(scientificName == bird_species)

brd_joineddata_model4$year_bout <- paste(brd_joineddata_model4$year, brd_joineddata_model4$boutNumber, sep = "_")

head(brd_joineddata_model4)

# Get all valid surveys years across sites (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  distinct(siteID, year, boutNumber)

# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a site* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model4 %>%
  group_by(siteID, year_bout) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")


# Get all valid surveys years across sites (so we can fill in NAs)
valid_site_years <- brd_perpoint_clean %>%
  filter(siteID %in% small_sites) %>%
  distinct(siteID, year, boutNumber)

valid_site_years$year_bout <- paste(valid_site_years$year, valid_site_years$boutNumber, sep = "_")
valid_site_years_bout <- subset(valid_site_years, select = -c(year, boutNumber))


# Get detections — only species *actually observed at a site* (so we can fill in 0s)
detections <- brd_joineddata_model4 %>%
  group_by(siteID, year_bout) %>%
  summarize(present = 1, .groups = "drop")

# Join and fill
site_by_year <- valid_site_years_bout %>%
  left_join(detections, by = c("siteID", "year_bout")) %>%
  mutate(present = replace_na(present, 0)) %>%
  
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year_bout,
    values_from = present
  )


head(site_by_year, n=10)
```

#### Create the Pao presence-absence object (Pao)
```{r}
birds_pao_model4 <- createPao(
  data = site_by_year[, c("2018_1", "2018_2","2019_1","2019_2", "2020_1","2020_2", "2021_1","2021_2", "2022_1", "2022_2", "2023_1", "2023_2")],
  nsurveyseason = c(2,2,2,2,2,2),
  unitnames = site_by_year$siteID,
  title = "Red-bellied Woodpecker"
)
```

#### Run the actual model
```{r}
birds_occupancy_model4 <- occMod(
  data = birds_pao_model4,           
  model = list(
    psi ~ 1,  
    epsilon ~ 1,
    gamma ~ 1,
    p ~ 1),
  type = 'do.1'
)

summary(birds_occupancy_model4)
```

#### Model Results

This shows that Melanerpes carolinus has an occupancy probability (psi) of % (i.e., if you go to any of these sites, there is a % chance of this bird occupying the site) and a detection probability (p) of % (i.e., if you visit a site and the bird occupies it, there is a % chance you will detect it)

```{r}
ests <- as.data.frame(print_one_site_estimates(mod = birds_occupancy_model4))

ests <- ests[1:4,] %>% 
  mutate(parm = c("psi", "gamma", "epsilon", "p")) %>% 
  select(parm, est, se, lower, upper) %>% 
  rename(., 
    c(
      Parameter = parm,
      Estimate = est,
      SE = se,
      L95 = lower,
      U95 = upper
    )
  ) %>% 
  `rownames<-`(seq_len(nrow(ests[1:4,])))

coef(birds_occupancy_model4, param = 'psi')
```


```{r}
ggplot(ests, aes(x = Parameter, y = Estimate)) +
  labs(x = "Parameter", y = "Estimate") +
  geom_bar(stat = 'identity') +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = L95, ymax = U95), width = 0.2) +
  theme_bw()
```
